headline: Cockenoe Reef on the Slack: Sea Bass Numbers Build Toward August
subhead: The neap tide easing in behind this week widens the strike window on the reef system, while the bass go quiet until dark.
body_markdown:
Tuesday morning I had a decision to make before I even left the dock — Cockenoe or Penfield. Both have been holding fish, but the reef you pick this time of year is a bet on current speed as much as anything else. With the first-quarter neap sliding in on the 21st and 22nd, I wanted the reef where a softer current works in my favor, not against me. Cockenoe's northeast drop, that 18-to-25-foot ledge off the back side of the island, fishes best when the drift is slow enough to keep a jig in the zone instead of skipping it across the rocks. So Cockenoe it was, and it paid off.

We flagged this last week — said sea bass would keep building through August — and that's exactly what's showing up on the reef. Fish to four pounds came off that ledge on half-ounce jigheads tipped with Gulp Sandworms and squid strips, worked on the last two hours of the incoming when the current finally settled enough to hold bottom without a heavier lead. The bite wasn't nonstop — you're picking through a lot of shorts to find the keepers — but the numbers are trending the right direction week over week, and with water in the western basin sitting warm (Kings Point read 72 degrees, a full two ticks above New London's 70), that thermal cushion should keep the sea bass pattern developing rather than stalling out.

Porgies are riding shotgun on the same structure. The Cows off Stamford and the flats tight to Greenwich Point are both loaded right now — sandworms and clam on a high-low rig, small hooks, light sinkers, anchored up rather than drifting. These fish don't need finesse, they need you in the right depth, and 15 to 20 feet over broken bottom is where they're stacking on the last of the ebb into dead low.

Fluke is the more dependable check-writer this week, and it's holding to structure the way it always does even with the Sound running warm. Penfield Reef and the channel edges off Sheffield Island are both producing on moving water — I want current, either tide, doesn't matter which, as long as it's pushing. Bucktails in the half-ounce to one-ounce range, white or chartreuse, tipped with a strip of Gulp, dragged slow along the drop-offs where the reef falls into 20 to 30 feet. Best fish this week went just over four pounds off Penfield on the outgoing, but the west end of my beat is fishing better than the east right now — that west-to-east temperature gradient across the Sound means the bait and the fluke that follow it are both a little more concentrated up here toward Greenwich and Norwalk than they are further out toward the Race.

Striped bass are the tough conversation this week, and I'm not going to dress it up. The pattern coastwide right now is nocturnal — warm, shallow water has pushed keeper-class bass onto a dawn, dusk, and after-dark clock, and Western Sound is no exception. Daytime trips around the Norwalk Islands and Sheffield Island are mostly quiet unless you catch a bluefish blitz pushing bait to the surface and a bass sneaks in underneath it. If you want a real shot at bass, you're fishing the last hour of light into full dark, working bunker chunks or live bait around the rips off Greenwich Point and Sheffield Island, or swimming an eel along the deeper edges of Cockenoe after the boat traffic clears out. It's a different game than June — slower, quieter, more patient — but the fish are there. I had two bass over 30 inches on chunked bunker at Sheffield Island Wednesday night, both after ten o'clock, both on the last of the ebb.

Bluefish are showing in pockets, not blitzes — schools riding bunker through the area, occasionally erupting off the Norwalk Islands or out toward the Cows. When you see the birds working, get on it fast with poppers or a straight metal like a Kastmaster, because these windows close in minutes, not hours. It's not the sustained daylight blitz you're hearing about further down the coast, but it's enough action to make a slow bass morning worth staying out for.

Weekend boat traffic is its own tide chart out here. Saturday and Sunday mid-day, the mooring fields off Norwalk and the channel into Sheffield Island turn into a highway, and it pushes fish off the shallower structure. My move is simple — fish the backside structure the pleasure boats ignore, or get out at first light and be off the water by nine, before the parade starts.

Looking ahead, the neap settling in over the next two days should widen the productive windows on every reef in the system — slower current means longer drifts and more time with your bait in the strike zone before you have to reset. I'd expect sea bass to keep climbing on Cockenoe and the Norwalk Islands structure, fluke to hold steady on Penfield and Sheffield as long as the water stays moving, and bass to stay a night bite until we get a real wind shift out of the northeast to knock the surface temperature down. If I had one trip to make this week, it'd be a night tide at Sheffield Island on the last of the ebb, bunker chunks soaking on the bottom, with a bucktail rod rigged and ready in case the fluke show up first.
